network.overall_strategy: Anchor threonine synthesis on the two experimentally supported endgames in the supplied literature: a surface cyanosulfidic nitrile sequence from lactaldehyde and a hydrothermal alanine plus formaldehyde aldol homologation. Build the alanine hub from three literature-guided upstream routes, allow formaldehyde either as an environmental pool or as a speculative hydrothermal CO2 reduction product, and allow lactaldehyde either as an environmental pool or as a speculative pyruvaldehyde reduction product. To stay within the requested graph size, ubiquitous water, ammonia, and H2 are treated as environmental reagents in mechanisms and conditions rather than as separate molecule nodes, and the target is represented without stereochemistry because the reported prebiotic routes do not resolve homochirality.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal reduction of carbon dioxide to formaldehyde

conditions.other: H2-rich alkaline vent fluid provides reducing power; H2 is treated as an environmental reagent rather than a standalone node; anoxic porewater

reactions.mechanism: Surface-bound CO2 is stepwise reduced through formyl-like intermediates to formaldehyde retained in porewater.
reactions.reasoning: Formaldehyde is the obligatory C1 electrophile in the alanine-formaldehyde route demonstrated by Aubrey et al. (2008). The curated review further notes hydrothermal CO2 reduction and Fischer-Tropsch-type chemistry on Fe and Ni-bearing surfaces as plausible formaldehyde sources, so this feeder step is chemically motivated but remains more speculative than the terminal aldol step (Aubrey et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Strecker formation of alanine nitrile from acetaldehyde

conditions.other: NH3-rich cyanosulfidic pool; dissolved ammonia is an environmental reagent rather than a standalone node; wet-dry concentration under anoxic conditions

reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde forms an imine or iminium with dissolved ammonia, then cyanide adds to give the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: The review identifies hydrolysis of 2-aminopropanenitrile as an alanine source in the cyanosulfidic network of Patel et al. (2015). Formation of that aminonitrile from acetaldehyde is the necessary upstream Strecker step, so this node is well grounded by the same chemistry even though the review emphasizes the hydrolysis product more than this precursor-forming step (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alanine nitrile to alanine

conditions.other: Hydrolytic wet phases in evaporitic pools; bulk water is solvent and reagent but is not a standalone node

reactions.mechanism: The nitrile hydrates to an amide and then hydrolyzes further to the carboxylic acid alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of 2-aminopropanenitrile to alanine is explicitly cited in the review as an upstream route to alanine in the Patel cyanosulfidic framework. Warm aqueous wet phases make aminonitrile-to-amino-acid conversion plausible under surface conditions (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Net cyanosulfidic synthesis of serine from glycolaldehyde

conditions.other: NH3-bearing cyanosulfidic pool; water and dissolved ammonia are environmental reagents rather than standalone nodes; wet-dry and UV-dark cycling under anoxic conditions

reactions.mechanism: A net sequence of cyanohydrin formation, ammonia incorporation, and nitrile hydrolysis converts glycolaldehyde into serine.
reactions.reasoning: The review states that the threonine sequence parallels a serine sequence from glycolaldehyde in the same cyanosulfidic protometabolism paper. This node intentionally collapses the documented cyanohydrin, aminonitrile, and hydrolysis substeps into one net serine-forming transformation to keep the network within the requested size while remaining literature-guided (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrothermal reduction of serine to alanine

conditions.other: Reduced subseafloor fluids supply reducing equivalents; moderate residence time favored to limit thermal degradation

reactions.mechanism: Hydrothermal deoxygenation of the serine side-chain hydroxymethyl group gives alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey et al. (2008) describe hydrothermal amino acid interconversions and specifically note serine reduction to alanine. Including this step links the surface serine pool to the hydrothermal alanine hub that feeds threonine, although moderate temperatures are preferred because hydroxy amino acids can also decompose under harsher vent conditions (Aubrey et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Iron-promoted reductive amination of pyruvate to alanine

conditions.other: Iron-rich anoxic hydrothermal porewater; hydroxylamine serves as nitrogen source and reactive intermediate donor

reactions.mechanism: Pyruvate condenses with hydroxylamine to an oxime or imino-like intermediate that is reduced by Fe0 and Fe2+ to alanine.
reactions.reasoning: The review cites Muchowska et al. (2019) for iron-promoted reductive amination of pyruvate with hydroxylamine to alanine at about 70 C. This provides an experimentally grounded, non-cyanide route into the alanine hub under reduced iron-rich hydrothermal conditions (Muchowska et al., 2019).

reactions.name: Reduction of pyruvaldehyde to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic reducing pool; reductive equivalents likely supplied by sulfide or photoredox chemistry but are not explicit nodes

reactions.mechanism: Reduction of the keto group of 2-oxopropanal yields the alpha-hydroxy aldehyde lactaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: The review identifies lactaldehyde availability as a key uncertainty and lists reduction of pyruvaldehyde as one plausible source. No direct threonine-specific experimental demonstration is provided in the supplied papers, so this upstream step is explicitly speculative; it is included because the Patel et al. (2015) surface route requires a chemically credible feeder to lactaldehyde.

reactions.name: Cyanohydrin formation from lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Cyanosulfidic surface pool; wet-dry concentration and dark intervals favor nitrile retention; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the aldehyde carbonyl of lactaldehyde and protonation yields the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support initiation of the surface threonine route by HCN addition to lactaldehyde. The curated summary appears to contain a carbon-count inconsistency for the cyanohydrin intermediate; addition of HCN to C3 lactaldehyde gives a chemically consistent C4 cyanohydrin, represented here as 2,3-dihydroxybutanenitrile, while preserving the experimentally supported reaction logic (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Amination of lactaldehyde cyanohydrin to threonine nitrile

conditions.other: NH3-rich aqueous film; dissolved ammonia is an environmental reagent rather than a standalone node; sheltered wet-dry cycling under anoxic conditions

reactions.mechanism: Dissolved ammonia converts the alpha-hydroxynitrile center into the corresponding alpha-aminonitrile while retaining the beta-hydroxyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Conversion of the lactaldehyde-derived cyanohydrin to the corresponding aminonitrile is the second step of the Patel threonine sequence. The review notes that aminonitrile stability under UV and fluctuating pool chemistry remains an open question, so sheltered wet-dry films are favored (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine nitrile to threonine

conditions.other: Hydrolytic wet phases in surface pools; bulk water is solvent and reagent but is not a standalone node

reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydration of the nitrile to an amide and then to the carboxylic acid yields threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanenitrile to threonine is the terminal Patel step. The review correctly emphasizes that this chemistry does not solve prebiotic homochirality and that the aminonitrile may be kinetically fragile, so the product is represented here as non-enantioenriched threonine (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Aldol homologation of alanine with formaldehyde

conditions.other: Subseafloor hydrothermal porewaters; moderate residence time favored to reduce threonine breakdown; anoxic

reactions.mechanism: An enol or carbanion equivalent at the alanine alpha-carbon adds to formaldehyde, and proton transfer furnishes the beta-hydroxy amino acid skeleton of threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey et al. (2008) experimentally demonstrated threonine formation from alanine and formaldehyde under submarine hydrothermal conditions. This aldol-type homologation is therefore one of the strongest anchors in the network, although the review notes ongoing questions about threonine thermal lability and possible allo-threonine or other side products, so moderate hydrothermal residence times are favored (Aubrey et al., 2008).

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker route to alanine, then homologation

pathways.name: Pyruvate hydroxylamine route to alanine, then homologation

pathways.name: Pyruvate hydroxylamine route with CO2-derived formaldehyde
pathways.description: Pyruvate is converted to alanine in iron-rich hydrothermal settings while the required formaldehyde is generated in-network from CO2 before the final aldol step.

pathways.name: Glycolaldehyde to serine to alanine, then homologation
pathways.description: Surface cyanosulfidic chemistry gives serine from glycolaldehyde, hydrothermal reduction converts serine to alanine, and alanine then undergoes formaldehyde homologation.

pathways.description: The serine-mediated alanine route is combined with hydrothermal CO2 reduction to furnish the formaldehyde required for the final threonine-forming aldol step.

pathways.name: Direct cyanosulfidic threonine route from lactaldehyde
pathways.description: Experimentally anchored surface pathway in which environmental lactaldehyde is converted through a cyanohydrin and aminonitrile to threonine.

pathways.name: Pyruvaldehyde-fed cyanosulfidic threonine route
pathways.description: A speculative upstream reduction supplies lactaldehyde from pyruvaldehyde, after which the literature-supported surface cyanohydrin and aminonitrile sequence yields threonine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Best-supported endgame and the strongest current path, although it is a module from the alanine hub rather than a full source-to-target route. rxn_011 is atom-balanced, directly aligned with the Aubrey hydrothermal alanine + formaldehyde homologation, and environmentally consistent. Remaining caveats are upstream precursor supply plus known literature issues of threonine selectivity and hydrothermal lability.
suggestions: Specify the hydrothermal temperature, pressure, and pH window for rxn_011.
Discuss expected threonine versus allo-threonine formation and threonine decomposition under hydrothermal conditions.
Connect this endgame to a balanced alanine-supply path if a full de novo route is intended.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The threonine-forming endgame rxn_011 is strong, but rxn_001 is a major conservation problem. CO2 -> CH2O is unbalanced as written and needs explicit reducing equivalents and coproducts, likely H2 in and H2O out, plus realistic vent catalysts. Formaldehyde generation from CO2 is plausible in hydrothermal settings but remains more speculative than the final homologation step, and alanine sourcing is still assumed rather than produced within this path.
suggestions: Rewrite rxn_001 with explicit redox stoichiometry, such as a justified H2-driven vent reduction scheme.
Specify Fe/Ni or other hydrothermal catalysts and reducing conditions for formaldehyde formation.
Address whether hydrothermal formaldehyde can accumulate to useful concentrations.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Conceptually coherent and literature-guided: Strecker-type alanine production followed by hydrothermal homologation. However, rxn_002 and rxn_003 are both conservation violations. Chemically, rxn_002 likely needs NH3 as reactant and H2O as product, and rxn_003 needs 2 H2O in and NH3 out. The path also implies surface-to-hydrothermal transfer of alanine without an explicit transport or concentration step.
suggestions: Add explicit NH3/H2O stoichiometry to the Strecker step in rxn_002.
Write rxn_003 as alanine nitrile + 2 H2O -> alanine + NH3.
Add or justify alanine transfer from surface pools to hydrothermal settings.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This extends P3 with in-network formaldehyde supply, but it inherits the Strecker/hydrolysis stoichiometric problems and adds the unbalanced and speculative rxn_001. rxn_001, rxn_002, and rxn_003 all need correction before the path is chemically defensible as a complete route.
suggestions: Correct rxn_001 with explicit hydrothermal redox bookkeeping.
Add NH3 and H2O explicitly to rxn_002 and 2 H2O/NH3 to rxn_003.
Make the surface-to-hydrothermal transport step explicit.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A reasonably coherent hydrothermal-only route combining Muchowska-style pyruvate-to-alanine chemistry with the Aubrey alanine-to-threonine homologation. The weakness is rxn_006: as written it is unbalanced and omits the reducing equivalents and iron redox bookkeeping needed for pyruvate + hydroxylamine -> alanine.
suggestions: Specify Fe0/Fe2+ participation and net redox stoichiometry for rxn_006.
State hydrothermal conditions near the reported iron-promoted regime.
Discuss whether hydroxylamine is available at the required concentration.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The alanine-to-threonine step remains strong, but both precursor-supply steps are weak as written. rxn_006 lacks explicit redox bookkeeping for iron-promoted reductive amination, and rxn_001 lacks the reductant and coproducts needed for CO2 reduction to formaldehyde.
suggestions: Balance rxn_006 with explicit redox partners and iron conditions.
Balance rxn_001 with explicit H2/H2O or another justified hydrothermal scheme.
Provide evidence that both alanine and formaldehyde can coexist in the same hydrothermal niche.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This path follows the literature logic well: cyanosulfidic serine production, hydrothermal serine-to-alanine reduction, then homologation. The main defects are stoichiometric. rxn_004 needs H2O as reactant to represent the net serine synthesis, and rxn_005 needs explicit redox bookkeeping, likely involving a reductant and H2O formation. Surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is also only implicit.
suggestions: Write rxn_004 as a balanced net reaction including H2O.
Specify the reductant and coproducts for rxn_005.
Add or justify transport of serine or alanine into the hydrothermal environment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P8 is conceptually reasonable but burdened by three flawed upstream steps. rxn_004, rxn_005, and rxn_001 are all unbalanced as written, so the path does not yet constitute a mass-conserving route from listed precursors to threonine.
suggestions: Add H2O to rxn_004.
Add explicit reductant and coproducts to rxn_005.
Rewrite rxn_001 with hydrothermal redox stoichiometry and catalyst context.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the most direct Patel-style surface endgame. rxn_008 is the best-specified surface step in the network: balanced and chemically sound. But rxn_009 and rxn_010 are conservation violations as written. Chemically, rxn_009 needs NH3 in and H2O out, while rxn_010 needs 2 H2O in and NH3 out. With those fixes, this would become a strong prebiotic threonine route.
suggestions: Add explicit NH3/H2O stoichiometry to rxn_009.
Write rxn_010 as threonine nitrile + 2 H2O -> threonine + NH3.
Clarify lactaldehyde source or concentration mechanism if it is treated as an environmental pool.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The downstream cyanosulfidic sequence matches the intended surface chemistry, but the speculative upstream supply step rxn_007 is both unbalanced and weakly justified. It likely needs H2 or another reductant. rxn_009 and rxn_010 still need explicit NH3/H2O stoichiometry.
suggestions: Balance rxn_007 with an explicit reductant and cite a plausible surface photoredox or mineral context.
Add NH3 and H2O explicitly to rxn_009.
Add 2 H2O in and NH3 out to rxn_010.

evaluation.network_feedback: Conceptually strong but not valid as written. The graph has enough nodes, is connected, and its route design aligns well with the Patel, Aubrey, and Muchowska literature. Representing threonine without stereochemistry is acceptable for this prebiotic context. However, the deterministic balance check flags 9 of 11 reactions as unbalanced; only rxn_008 and rxn_011 conserve atoms as written. Most failures arise because ubiquitous species were externalized from the node list but not from stoichiometric bookkeeping: rxn_003 and rxn_010 need 2 H2O in and NH3 out; rxn_004 needs H2O in; rxn_007 needs H2 in; rxn_009 and the Strecker form of rxn_002 need NH3 in and H2O out; rxn_001, rxn_005, and rxn_006 need explicit redox partners or products. Many of these are likely repairable, but until then the network is not mass-conserving. Environmental assignment is mostly sensible, but surface-to-hydrothermal transfer is implicit in P3, P4, P7, and P8, and the speculative rxn_001 and rxn_007 need clearer catalyst and condition support. The network also does not yet engage key literature caveats around formaldehyde concentration, lactaldehyde availability, threonine selectivity, and hydrothermal threonine instability. Best current path is P1 because rxn_011 is balanced and experimentally supported; P9 would become a strong complete route if rxn_009 and rxn_010 were corrected. Overall, this network is not approved as written.
